source: For example, if a wine has an alcohol level of 12 it has an 86% probability of being good.
why: This probability is read off the story's fitted logistic model, whose coefficients are not in data/winedata.csv; refitting a logistic regression of the data's quality_binary on alcohol does not give 86% (it gives about 35%), and a plain pandas computation on the provided file cannot reproduce the story's figure.

source: It's only 5% full — which means its physiochemical properties indicate only a 5% chance of it being good. This is what you get when taking the average value for each wine property, represented by the vertical line in the distribution chart below.
why: The 5% is the story's logistic model evaluated at the mean of every predictor; producing it needs the model weights and intercept (data/model-weights.csv and data/model-intercept.csv in the project repository), which are not among the provided files.

source: In this case, Alcohol appears to have the biggest impact on Quality, followed by Volatile Acidity and the amount of sulphates in the wine.
why: This ranking comes from a Random Forest variable-importance table (data/importance.csv in the project repository), which is not among the provided files; data/winedata.csv alone holds the wines, not the model's importance scores.

source: This is low for reds, which tend to be between 12 and 15%.
why: A general statement about red wines from an external source, not a quantity measured in data/winedata.csv.
